stemMd:
Shepherds in the mountain valleys of Esk communicate across long distances in a whistled form of their spoken language. Whistled Esk reproduces the rises and falls in pitch of spoken words but not their vowels and consonants, so many different words sound alike when whistled. Linguist Teodor Malm recorded 200 whistled messages and played them to experienced listeners. Listeners correctly understood 95 percent of the messages about routine matters, such as when to bring the flocks down, but only 40 percent of the messages about unexpected events, such as a fallen bridge. Because the two kinds of messages used words of similar length and similar pitch patterns, Malm concludes that ______

Which choice most logically completes the text?

options.label: A
options.textMd: listeners rely heavily on knowing what a message is likely to say in order to understand whistled Esk.

options.label: B
options.textMd: whistled Esk is less useful than spoken Esk for passing routine information from one shepherd to another.

options.label: C
options.textMd: listeners understand whistled Esk mainly by recognizing the distinctive pitch pattern of each individual word.

options.label: D
options.textMd: messages about unexpected events tend to contain longer words than messages about routine matters do.

explanationMd:
Read the last sentence as an experiment's logic. Two kinds of messages produced very different results (95 percent understood versus 40 percent). The sentence then rules out two possible reasons for the gap: the messages did not differ in word length or in pitch patterns. So the explanation has to be something else that differs between routine and unexpected messages.

The passage has already supplied it. Because whistling drops vowels and consonants, many words sound alike, so a listener cannot decode a message from the sounds alone and must fill the gaps from what the message is probably about. Routine messages are predictable; unexpected ones are not. That is why the conclusion that listeners rely heavily on knowing what a message is likely to say completes the text.

The most tempting wrong answer says listeners decode each word's pitch pattern. Check it against the data: the pitch patterns were similar in both kinds of message, yet understanding was very different, so pitch recognition cannot be what mainly drives success. It is close to the opposite of the conclusion the result supports.

distractorRationale.c: If listeners mainly recognized each word's pitch pattern, messages with similar pitch patterns should have been understood about equally well. They were not (95 versus 40 percent), and the passage adds that many words sound alike when whistled, so this explanation is the one the evidence undercuts.
distractorRationale.d: The final sentence states that the two kinds of messages used words of similar length, so this contradicts the passage directly.
distractorRationale.b: Listeners understood 95 percent of routine messages, and the passage never compares whistled with spoken Esk on accuracy. Nothing supports the claim that whistling is worse for routine information; if anything, it works well for it.

accessibilityText: A short linguistics passage. Shepherds in the mountain valleys of Esk communicate across long distances in a whistled form of their language. Whistled Esk reproduces the pitch rises and falls of spoken words but not their vowels and consonants, so many different words sound alike when whistled. Linguist Teodor Malm recorded 200 whistled messages and played them to experienced listeners. Listeners correctly understood 95 percent of messages about routine matters, such as when to bring the flocks down, but only 40 percent of messages about unexpected events, such as a fallen bridge. The final sentence reads: because the two kinds of messages used words of similar length and similar pitch patterns, Malm concludes that, blank. The choices are: listeners rely heavily on knowing what a message is likely to say in order to understand whistled Esk; whistled Esk is less useful than spoken Esk for passing routine information between shepherds; listeners understand whistled Esk mainly by recognizing the distinctive pitch pattern of each individual word; and messages about unexpected events tend to contain longer words than messages about routine matters.

provenance.notes: Original inference item. Esk, its whistled form and Malm's study are invented. The passage controls for word length and pitch pattern, so the key is the remaining explanation; the strongest distractor is the one the control rules out.

review.author: sat-wave8-rw-author

independentSolve.workingNotes: Since whistling makes many words sound alike and the two message types were acoustically similar, the gap (95% vs 40%) must come from listeners' expectations about content. Routine messages were understood very well, so 'less useful for routine information' fails; recognizing each word's distinctive pitch pattern is contradicted by words sounding alike; longer words contradicts 'similar length'. [A second, separate blind solve (blind-reviewer-wave8-sat-rw-run1) reached the same answer: Since word length and pitch patterns were similar for both kinds of messages, the comprehension gap (95% vs 40%) must come from predictability: listeners rely on expecting the content. No comparison with spoken Esk is given; recognizing pitch patterns would not explain the gap given similar patterns; similar word length contradicts the longer-words option.]
